newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dlr higher, but locked in ranges by Tokyo noon.
newsitem.headline: Dlr higher, but locked in ranges by Tokyo noon.

text.p: The dollar was higher against the yen by Tokyo noon on Friday after biding time in a narrow range before meetings between U.S. and Japanese officials later in the day and among Group of Seven (G7) nations on Sunday.
The business suspension of a Japanese life insurer prompted dollar buying, but its upward march was later halted by talk of a heavy amount of options-related sales above 126.50 yen.
The Ministry of Finance said on Friday it had ordered Nissan Mutual Life Insurance Co to halt some of its operations.
Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said Nissan Life's failure was due to its failed asset management, but added there would be no similar cases with other life insurance firms.

This news, coupled with expectations of commercial dollar buying at 0100 GMT, lifted the dollar above 126.30 yen in early trade. Despite Mitsuzuka's remarks, dealers said they would not rule out more failures at smaller insurers. "I think that Nissan Life's failure is just the prelude to more revelations of problems in the insurance industry," said one bank trader.

The news lifted the dollar up, but only fleetingly, dealers said. "Speculation also rose that it might sell off its overseas assets, which would be a yen-buying factor," said a dealer at a European bank.
Dealers said combined heavy selling demand from Japanese exporters and options-related sales weighed on the dollar.

They said there were short-term exotic options positions in the market, with large positions of so-called "reverse knock-out" options thought to have been taken with strike prices around 124 yen and knock-out prices of 127 to 127.30 yen.

Holders of the options are rumoured to be selling the dollar when it nears 127 yen, in order to prevent their option positions from being knocked out, and this is helping to cap the dollar's moves against the yen, dealers said.
One dealer estimated that the total of options-linked sales above 126.50 yen may amount to several billion dollars, although some of the options will mature in the near term.

Traders were preoccupied with Sunday's Group of Seven nations' meeting, with the focus on whether the G7 nations will issue strong currency statements and deem the yen's fall against the dollar as excessive.

"If the G7 issues strong currency statements by deeming the yen's fall against the dollar as excessive, that would have some impact in pushing the dollar down versus the yen on Monday," said another dealer at a European bank.
But some dealers said it may be difficult to single out the dollar/yen among the various currencies and issues to be discussed at the G7 meeting.
